opus-5.5.text:
I think 43% is actually low. Look at how fast this field has moved. A few years ago, the idea that an AI system could solve olympiad problems at gold-medal level seemed far off, and now that's been done, with formally verified proofs in some cases. Millennium Prize problems are obviously a different beast. They're not just hard competition problems; some of them may require entirely new mathematical frameworks. But I think people underestimate what happens when you combine the scale of search these systems can do with formal verification.

The key thing for me is verification. Once you have a system that can write proofs in something like Lean, you no longer have to trust the model. You can check the output mechanically. That changes the dynamics completely, because you can let the system explore a huge number of directions, fail most of the time, and only keep what's provably correct. Human mathematicians can't operate that way. They have limited time and attention.

There's also the question of timing. These problems have stood for decades, and the base rate of any of them being solved in a given year is low. So whatever gets solved next will probably not be solved for a while. The longer that gap, the more likely AI plays a significant role, because the capabilities are compounding. Even if a human gets the key insight, I'd expect AI to be deeply involved in checking lemmas, exploring special cases, and formalizing the argument. By that definition of "significant assistance," I'd put the number well above 43%.

The honest uncertainty is whether some of these problems need a conceptual leap, a new way of seeing the problem, that current approaches can't produce. That's a real open question. But I'd bet on the systems getting there, and I'd bet on it happening sooner than most mathematicians expect.

r002.rationale: The response says the next solution will probably not happen for a while and expects AI to play a significant role; it does not predict a near-future solution without significant AI assistance.

r003.rationale: The response discusses the next Millennium Prize problem, but makes no prediction about the second problem solved from now.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think 43% is probably in the right ballpark, but I'd want to pull apart what "significant AI assistance" means, because that phrase is doing a lot of work.

If you mean the AI produces the proof end to end, or produces the key idea that the human then writes up, I'd put the number lower than that for the very next Millennium problem that falls. Those problems are hard in a specific way. It's not that there are a lot of steps; it's that nobody knows what the right framework even is. The Poincaré conjecture needed Perelman to understand Ricci flow with surgery at a level that didn't exist before. That's not search over a known space, that's inventing the space. Current systems, including the ones we build at Harmonic, are very strong at the search part and still weak at the "what should the objects even be" part.

But if "significant assistance" includes a mathematician using a model to check thousands of lemmas, to formalize their argument in Lean so they can trust it, to run through case analyses that would have taken a grad student six months, then I think 43% is too low. By the time one of these gets solved, I'd be surprised if the person doing it wasn't leaning on these tools heavily, just the way nobody today proves something without a computer algebra system within reach. In that sense the forecast is almost a question about timing. If the next one falls in the next two or three years, it's probably mostly human. If it falls in ten, it's almost certainly human plus AI in a deep way.

The thing I'd really watch isn't the Millennium problems at all. It's the layer below them. Can a system autonomously close out open problems in a well-defined subfield, things that are real research questions but where the framework exists? We're starting to see that happen. Once that's routine, the gap to the big problems is narrower than people think, because a lot of what makes those problems hard is just the sheer volume of technical work surrounding the one creative leap. Compress that volume and you've changed who can even attempt them.

So, 43%? Fine as a number. I'd just say the uncertainty is less about whether AI will be involved and more about whether we'll agree, after the fact, on how much credit it deserves.

r001.rationale: The candidate says 43% is too low only if “significant assistance” includes extensive tool use, but otherwise calls it lower than the estimate or says 43% is in the right ballpark. It does not clearly judge the stated forecast to be an underestimate.

r002.rationale: The candidate says a problem solved in the next two or three years would probably be mostly human, but does not say that a solution without significant AI assistance would probably need to happen that soon.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses the next problem and possible timing, but makes no prediction about the second Millennium Prize problem solved from now.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s plausible, but a lot depends on what you mean by “significant AI assistance.” There’s a big difference between an AI independently producing the key insight and a mathematician using AI to explore examples, check arguments, or work through technical details. Those are very different levels of capability, and the forecast bundles them together.

The other important thing is that this is about the next solution, without a fixed deadline. If that solution is many years away, there’s a lot of time for AI tools to become part of how mathematicians work. So I wouldn’t interpret 43% as a prediction that an autonomous AI mathematician is imminent. I’d interpret it as a plausible bet that AI will play a meaningful role in a major mathematical discovery.

r001.rationale: The response calls 43% plausible, but does not say the probability is too low or an underestimate.

r002.rationale: It does not predict that an unaided human solution would need to happen very soon; it instead notes the next solution could be many years away.

r003.rationale: It discusses the next solution and says AI involvement is a plausible bet, but does not predict that the second problem solved from now will probably involve AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hard part is defining “significant AI assistance.” There’s a big difference between an AI producing the central insight and a mathematician using AI to explore examples, check an argument, or work through a technical step. Those are very different predictions bundled into one number.

If you mean that AI will play a meaningful role in the next solution, 43% seems plausible to me. If you mean that an AI will autonomously solve one of these problems, I’d be much more cautious. And this is a race: a human could already be close to solving one before AI reaches that level.

So I wouldn’t put too much weight on the precise percentage. The question I’d focus on is whether these systems can reliably help mathematicians make progress on problems where nobody knows the answer.
